passages.title: The great news the deniers dispute
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open Sūrah al-Nabaʼ with a single dramatic scene: the people of Makkah are buzzing with questions about one subject — the Day of Judgement — and Allah interrupts their chatter with a question of His own, names what they are really asking about, and then issues a doubled warning. What holds the passage together is this movement from *their* question (ayah 1) to *Allah's* answer (ayat 2–3) to His verdict on the whole exercise (ayat 4–5).

## The scene behind the question

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that when the revelation of the Qurʼān began, the pagan Arabs used to form circles to discuss and criticise it — especially its tremendous claims about Resurrection and Judgement. To them the idea seemed impossible, and it became the subject of protracted discussion: some believed it, others persuaded themselves that the predicted event would never take place. Some commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, add that their enquiry was not a sincere search for truth at all; they asked half-mockingly and half in doubt — when will this loudly proclaimed event actually happen?

That is the setting into which ayah 1 lands: *ʿamma yatasāʼalūn* — "What are they asking one another about?" Ibn Kathir explains that the question comes **in rejection of** the idolators' questioning, because it flowed from their denial. The sūrah does not open by patiently entertaining their enquiry; it opens, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, by shunning both the enquirers and the enquiry, expressing wonder that anyone should raise doubts about Resurrection and Judgement at all.

## The language: ʿamma and nabaʼ

Two words carry the weight of the opening.

**ʿAmma** (ayah 1) is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, a fusion of two particles: the preposition *ʿan* ("about") and the interrogative *mā* ("what?"), with the final letter of *mā* dropped in the compressed form. The sense is simply: "About what are they asking each other?" — and the beauty of the opening is that Allah Himself then supplies the answer.

**Nabaʼ** (ayah 2) is usually translated "news", but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that not every piece of news qualifies as *nabaʼ*. The word means momentous news of a great event — and here it is further magnified by the adjective *al-ʿaẓīm*, "the great". This refers to the news of the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir unpacks what "great" means in this context: dreadful, horrifying, overwhelming information.

## "About which they disagree" — ayah 3

Ibn Kathir explains that people were divided into two camps over this news: those who believe in it and those who disbelieve in it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms the same picture among the inhabitants of Makkah — some believed in Resurrection, others did not. Ayah 3 thus captures the human condition the sūrah is addressing: the greatest fact of the future had become a matter of dispute, argued back and forth in circles rather than faced.

## The doubled warning — ayat 4 and 5

Allah's reply to all this disputation is not an argument but a verdict, delivered twice: *kallā sa-yaʿlamūn, thumma kallā sa-yaʿlamūn* — "But no! They will come to know. Again, no! They will come to know."

The particle **kallā**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is a negative meaning "never, by no means". Its force here is that this matter cannot be understood by question and answer, by disputation and debate. Its reality will be understood only when they face it — a reality that leaves no room for questions, disputation, or denial. When they die, they will discover the realities of the next world; they will see the horrors of the Hereafter with their own eyes. The statement is asserted twice for emphasis. Ibn Kathir reads the pair of ayat the same way: a severe threat and a direct warning from Allah to those who deny the Day of Judgement.

## Where the passage leads

These five ayat are the doorway to the rest of the sūrah, and both commentaries note where it goes next. Ibn Kathir writes that Allah then begins to explain His great ability to create strange things and amazing matters, bringing this as proof of His ability to do whatever He wishes concerning the matter of the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the Qurʼān goes on to point to different demonstrations of His power in creation, to prove that it is not impossible for Allah to destroy this entire world and re-create it once again. So the passage does not leave the deniers with a bare threat; the sūrah turns next to the evidence.

## Living it

The passage draws a quiet but firm line between two ways of relating to ultimate realities: sincere enquiry that seeks the truth, and the half-mocking, half-doubting questioning of the Makkan circles that the sūrah shuns. It asks the believer to take the Day of Judgement as what it truly is — *al-nabaʼ al-ʿaẓīm*, the momentous news — not as one more topic to argue about, and to remember that certainty about it will come to every person in the end: better to meet that day having believed the news than to "come to know" only when knowing can no longer help.

passages.title: Signs of divine power in creation
passages.tafsir:
## Ten questions with one answer

Ayat 6–16 are a single sweeping argument. The sūrah opened with the idolators questioning one another about "the great news" — the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir explains that this questioning arose from their denial of its occurrence, and that Allah answered it with "a severe threat and a direct warning": "Nay, they will come to know! Nay, again, they will come to know!" (ayat 4–5). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of the particle *kallā* here: this is a matter that cannot be understood by question and answer or by disputation and debate — its reality will be understood by them when they face it, when they see the horrors of the Hereafter with their own eyes.

Then, instead of prolonging the debate, the passage turns their eyes to the world around them. In ten rapid strokes it moves from the earth beneath their feet to the mountains, to their own bodies, their sleep, the night and day, the sky, the sun, the rain, and finally the grain and gardens the rain brings forth. Ibn Kathir states the logic plainly: Allah "begins to explain His great ability to create strange things and amazing matters," bringing this as proof of His ability to do whatever He wishes "concerning the matter of the Hereafter and other matters as well." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way: these are demonstrations of power proving that it is not impossible for Allah to destroy this entire world and re-create it once again.

## The earth made ready (ayat 6–7)

The earth is called a **mihād** — a bed, something smoothed out and spread for rest. Ibn Kathir explains: an established, firm, and peaceful resting place made subservient to its inhabitants. The image is deliberate. A bed is prepared *for* someone; the earth did not merely happen to be habitable — it was made so.

The mountains are its **awtād**, pegs — the word used for the stakes that pin a tent to the ground. Ibn Kathir writes that Allah made them as pegs "to hold it in place, make it stable and firm... so that it may be suitable for dwelling and not quake with those who are in it." Bed and pegs together: a dwelling deliberately steadied for its occupants.

## The gift folded into your own life (ayat 8–11)

From the earth, the passage turns to the human being himself. "And We have created you in pairs" (ayah 8) — male and female, as Ibn Kathir says, "both of them enjoying each other, and by this means procreation is achieved." He connects it to the famous ayah of Sūrat al-Rūm: Allah created for you spouses from among yourselves "that you may find repose in them, and He has put between you affection and mercy" (30:21). Even human companionship is listed among the proofs of divine power.

**Sleep (ayah 9).** The word for rest here is **subāt**, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up its root: it comes from *sabt*, "to cut off." Sleep is a cutting-off — Ibn Kathir calls it "a cessation of movement" — and Maʿārif adds that it cuts off the worries and tensions a person carries, giving a rest nothing else can give. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then dwells on sleep as a great divine gift, and the reflection deserves to be heard in full force: sleep is given equally and simultaneously to all — rich and poor, learned and unlettered, kings and labourers. It does not depend on mattresses, pillows, or comfortable homes; often the poor labourer sleeps soundly in the open while the man of means suffers insomnia and reaches for pills that may not even work. It is given free, without being earned, to humans and animals alike — and it is *imposed* by Allah's mercy, so that even the one who wants to keep working is overtaken by it, his tiredness removed so he can work again. A blessing you cannot buy and cannot refuse.

**Night as a garment (ayah 10).** The night is a **libās**, a covering — "its shade and darkness covers the people," says Ibn Kathir, comparing it to "By the night as it conceals it" (91:4). Qatadah commented that it means "a tranquil residence." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easily missed: Allah did not only give man sleep, He built the *conditions* for sleep into the world itself — the darkness, the quiet, and the fact that sleep descends on humans and animals together, so that the whole world falls still at once. If people slept in scattered shifts, no one would ever have real peace.

**Day as livelihood (ayah 11).** And the counterpart: the day is **maʿāsh**, the arena of livelihood — made "radiant, luminous, and shining," in Ibn Kathir's words, so that people can come and go for their earning and business. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking observation: sleep alone would not be mercy. If the world were all night and man slept on forever, "the sleep will turn into death." Night and day are a matched pair, a cloak and a workplace, and the comfort of life is complete only with both.

## The sky and its lamp (ayat 12–13)

The gaze now lifts upward. "And We have built above you seven strong" — the seven heavens, which Ibn Kathir describes in their "vastness, loftiness, perfection, precision, and adornment with both stable and moving stars."

Within them, "a shining lamp" — the **sirāj wahhāj**, the blazing sun "that gives light to all of the world," as Ibn Kathir says. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the ordering of the passage here: having listed the comforts of the earth, attention is drawn to the comforts that come from the sky, and the most useful thing in the sky is the light of the sun — while among the useful things below the sky, the most beneficial and essential is the raining cloud, which comes next.

## Rain, and what rises from it (ayat 14–16)

**Al-muʿṣirāt (ayah 14).** Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities on this word: Ibn ʿAbbās — in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — said it means the clouds, and this was also the view of ʿIkrimah, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, al-Rabiʿ bin Anas, and al-Thawri, and the interpretation preferred by Ibn Jarir. Al-Farrāʼ sharpened the image: they are clouds *filled* with rain that have not yet released it — like a woman called *muʿṣir* when her cycle approaches but has not yet begun. The word catches the cloud at the moment of fullness, heavy and about to pour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, which renders *muʿṣirāt* as "rain-laden clouds," adds a harmonising note: this ayah shows rain coming from the clouds, while other ayat speak of rain from the *samāʼ* (sky); those verses probably refer to the upper atmosphere, a sense in which the Qurʼan uses *samāʼ* in many places.

**Thajjāj.** The water is *thajjāj* — Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Rabiʿ bin Anas said "poured out"; al-Thawri said "continuous"; Ibn Zayd said "abundant." Ibn Kathir supports this range of meaning from usage in the Sunnah: in the hadith of the woman with prolonged menstrual bleeding, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ suggested she dress the area with an absorbent cloth, and she replied that the bleeding was too much for that — "it flows profusely (*thajja*)." The word, then, means a gushing, unstinting downpour — all three meanings at once.

**And the purpose (ayat 15–16).** The rain is not an end in itself: "That We may produce therewith grain and plants, and gardens that are *alfāf*." Ibn Kathir unpacks the sequence: **grain** is what can be stored for humans and cattle; **vegetation** is what is eaten fresh; and the **gardens** are orchards of varied fruits, colors, tastes, and fragrances — even when gathered in a single plot of earth. *Alfāf*, said Ibn ʿAbbās and others, means "gathered" — dense, intertwined orchards. Ibn Kathir hears in this an echo of Sūrat al-Raʿd: neighboring tracts and gardens "watered with the same water, yet some of them We make more excellent than others to eat — verily, in these things there are signs for people who understand" (13:4). One water, endless variety — and, in the words of that ayah, signs for people who understand.

## Where the argument lands

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that having mentioned these divine blessings, the sūrah now reverts to its original theme — the Resurrection and Judgement, which arrives in the very next ayah. That is the key to reading this passage rightly. It is not a nature poem; it is evidence entered against denial. Every item in the list is something the deniers themselves lived inside daily — the ground they walked, the sleep that overcame them, the rain that fed them. Ibn Kathir's framing holds it all together: these wonders are brought forward as proof of Allah's ability to do whatever He wishes concerning the matter of the Hereafter, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the conclusion just as plainly — it is not impossible for the One who made all this to destroy this entire world and re-create it once again. The passage asks the believer to do what the deniers refused: to look at the utterly ordinary — a night's sleep, a heavy cloud, a dense orchard — and see in it the power and deliberate mercy of the One who will just as surely bring about the Day these ayat were revealed to affirm.

passages.title: The Day of Decision and cosmic upheaval
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat announce, with total certainty, the event the whole sūrah has been building toward: the Day of Decision — the Day of Judgement — is at a fixed time, with a set appointment, and when it arrives the most solid features of our world will simply give way. The passage moves in a deliberate sequence: the appointment is set (ayah 17), the Trumpet sounds and humanity streams forth (ayah 18), the sky itself opens up (ayah 19), and the mountains dissolve into what looks like a mirage (ayah 20). What holds the unit together is a single idea: the Day is not a vague possibility but a scheduled reality, and on that Day everything we treat as permanent proves temporary.

## An appointment that cannot be moved

Ayah 17 calls it *yawm al-faṣl* — "the Day of Decision" — and says it *kāna mīqātan*, "is an appointed time." Ibn Kathir explains that this Day, which is the Day of Judgement, is at a fixed time, with a set appointment: "Its time cannot be added to or decreased. No one knows its exact time except Allah." He connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And We delay it only for a term fixed" (11:104).

Two truths sit side by side here, and both matter. The Day is absolutely certain — the appointment is already set. And the Day is absolutely hidden — its exact moment belongs to Allah's knowledge alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms the same point simply: the Day of Decision refers to the Day of Resurrection, and it is a fixed appointment.

## The Trumpet and the crowds

Ayah 18 describes what happens when the appointment falls due: "the Day the Trumpet will be blown, and you will all come forth in crowds." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that other verses indicate the Trumpet will be blown twice: at the first blast the entire world comes to an end; at the second, the people of the entire world — the earlier generations and the later ones alike — are resurrected and come "in multitudes and droves."

Ibn Kathir cites a remarkable hadith here, reported by al-Bukhari in explanation of this very ayah. Abu Hurayrah relates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "That which is between the two blowings is forty." People pressed Abu Hurayrah — forty days? forty months? forty years? — and each time he refused to specify, saying "no comment." Then he continued with the Prophet's ﷺ words: "Then Allah will send down a rain from the sky and the dead body will sprout just as a green plant sprouts. Every part of the last person will deteriorate except for one bone, and it is the coccyx bone (tailbone). From it the creation will be assembled on the Day of Judgement."

What are the "crowds" (*afwājan*)? The early commentators offered complementary readings. Mujahid said it means "groups after groups." Ibn Jarir explained that each nation will come with its Messenger, connecting it to the ayah, "The Day when We shall call together all human beings with their Imam" (17:71). And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a hadith reported by Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, may Allah be pleased with him: the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection people will come in three different groups — one arriving at the Plain of Gathering fed, clothed, and mounted; another arriving barefoot; and a third dragged upon their faces. (Mazhari cites Nasa'i, Hakim and Baihaqi for this report.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some narratives mention ten types of groups, and that some scholars reconcile these by saying the groups will be divided according to people's deeds and character — the narratives do not conflict, and all of them may be true. The picture that emerges is sobering: on that Day, *how* you arrive is itself a verdict on how you lived.

## The sky becomes gates

Ayah 19: "The sky will be split open, becoming many gates." Ibn Kathir explains this concisely: the heaven will become "paths, and routes for the descending of the angels." On that Day the sky opens into gates, and through those openings the angels descend.

## Mountains like a mirage

Ayah 20 delivers the passage's most arresting image: "the mountains will be blown away, becoming like a mirage." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks both key words. *Suyyirat*, "set in motion," signifies that the mountains — mankind's very byword for firmness and strength — will be shifted from their positions and become like little particles of dust flying about in the atmosphere. And *sarāb* literally carries the sense of "to disappear"; it refers to the mirage, the optical illusion of a sheet of water that appears in the desert — from a distance it seems to be water, but when a person draws near, it vanishes. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the lexicons Sihah and Raghib for this.)

Ibn Kathir draws out exactly this meaning: the mountains "appear to the one who looks at them as if they are something, but they are actually nothing. After this they will be completely removed. Nothing will be seen of them, and there will be neither base nor trace of them." He reads this ayah alongside the Qur'an's other mountain-scenes on that Day: "You will see the mountains and think them solid, but they shall pass away as the passing away of the clouds" (27:88); "the mountains will be like carded wool" (101:5); "My Lord will blast them and scatter them as particles of dust. Then He shall leave them as a level smooth plain. You will see therein nothing crooked or curved" (20:105–107); and "the Day We shall cause the mountains to pass away, and you will see the earth as a leveled plain" (18:47). Read together, these verses trace a progression: the mountains move like clouds, loosen like wool, scatter like dust, and finally leave behind a perfectly level earth with no trace that they ever stood.

## Taking it to heart

The passage asks the reader to hold one thought steadily: the appointment is already fixed. Its date cannot be advanced or postponed, and no one but Allah knows when it falls — so the only uncertainty left is not *whether* we will stand in those crowds, but in *which* crowd we will arrive. And it dismantles our instinctive trust in permanence. If the sky can become open gates, and if the mountains — the very measure of solidity — can prove to be no more than a mirage that vanishes as you approach, then nothing in this world is as fixed as it looks. Only the appointment is fixed. This passage's work is done once the reader feels the ground shift: the Day is real, its time is set, and every human being will answer the summons.

passages.title: Hell's ambush and the transgressors' recompense
passages.tafsir:
## Where the transgressors' road ends

After the sūrah's sweeping scene of the Day of Decision — the Trumpet, the crowds, the heaven opened as gates, the mountains dissolved into mirage (ayat 17–20) — this passage answers the question that scene forces on every listener: *where does it all lead?* Ayat 21–30 are one tightly woven answer for those who spent their lives in rebellion: Hell is already waiting for them (21–22), their stay is measured in ages beyond counting (23), their food and drink are described (24–25), and then — crucially — the passage names the *justice* of it all (26) and the inner crime that earned it (27–28), before closing with the most terrifying sentence the Qur'an contains for the people of the Fire (29–30). What holds it together is the idea of exact correspondence: the punishment is not arbitrary but a mirror of the deed, "an exact recompense".

## Hell lying in ambush (ayat 21–22)

The passage opens with a startling image: **"Indeed, Hell is lying in ambush"** (ayah 21). The word *mirṣād* means an ambush — lying in wait to attack unawares, a hidden position for a surprise strike. Ibn Kathir explains it simply: Hell is "waiting in preparation." The image is deliberately unsettling. The transgressor walks through life assuming the road ahead is open; in reality something has been stationed on that road, watching, prepared.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, fills in the picture: the "ambush" refers to the bridge of Hell, where the angels will lie in wait — the angels of punishment to seize the inmates of Hell in a surprise attack, and the angels of reward to receive the people of Paradise and escort them to their abode. Hasan al-Baṣrī said there will be an outpost of guardian angels on that bridge: whoever carries a permit to enter Paradise passes; whoever does not is stopped (as recorded by Qurtubi). So — as Maʿārif notes on ayah 22 — the ambush itself is set for *everyone*, good and bad alike, since all must cross; but Hell is a *home* only for the transgressors.

Who are these transgressors? The word *ṭāghīn* comes from *ṭughyān*, "rebellion": a *ṭāghī* is one who exceeds the limit in disobeying the authority of Allah. Ibn Kathir describes them as "the disobedient rejectors who oppose the Messengers." Maʿārif observes that such total rebellion is possible only when a person abandons faith itself, so the primary reference is to the disbelievers — though it may extend, Mazhari adds, to groups who deviated from the limits of the Qur'an and Sunnah without expressly adopting disbelief. And for them Hell is a *maʼāb* — Ibn Kathir unpacks this word as "a place of return, final destination, final outcome, and residence." Not a station on the way; the end of the road itself.

## Ages upon ages (ayah 23)

**"They will abide therein for aḥqāb"** — endless ages. Here the scholars slowed down, because a single word carries enormous weight. *Aḥqāb* is the plural of *ḥiqbah* (in Ibn Kathir's spelling, *ḥuqb*), meaning a long stretch of time. How long? The early authorities gave staggering calculations. Ibn Jarir records from ʿAlī that one *ḥiqbah* is eighty years, each year twelve months, each month thirty days — and each day equivalent to a thousand years of our reckoning. Abu Hurairah, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas and others said seventy years rather than eighty, with the same reckoning. In the Musnad of Bazzar, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar traces to the Prophet ﷺ the report that those put in Hell for their sins will not come out until they tarry there for aḥqāb — one ḥiqbah being a little over eighty years, each year three hundred and sixty days by our reckoning. Maʿārif is careful here: the narratives conflict in their figures, and where they conflict one cannot settle on a number — but their common denominator stands firm: a *ḥiqbah* is an extremely long period of time. Hence Baidawi's rendering: "many long periods of time successively following the others."

But this word raised a real theological question, and the sources treat it honestly. If a *ḥiqbah* — however vast — is finite, does the punishment of the disbelievers eventually end? Maʿārif answers with the express texts of the Qur'an — *khālidīna fīhā abadā*, "they shall remain therein forever" — and the consensus of the Ummah that neither will Hell perish nor will the disbelievers ever be released. The ayah simply does not say what happens *after* the aḥqāb; it does not promise release. Hasan al-Baṣrī and Saʿīd ibn Jubair both explained *aḥqāb* as time with no end: whenever one age finishes, another begins, and so on without limit — Qatadah said the same, as Ibn Kathir records: "Whenever one era comes to an end, a new era follows it."

The scholars did register other readings, and the sources give them with their names. Ibn Kathir mentions — and Qurtubi supported, and Mazhari adopted — the possibility that *ṭāghīn* here refers not to disbelievers but to people of Tawhid (those who affirmed Allah's oneness) who fell into deviant beliefs without crossing into open disbelief: they would abide for the aḥqāb and then be discharged by virtue of their creed. Khalid bin Maʿdan similarly held that this ayah concerns the people of Tawhid. But Abu Hayyan objected decisively from the passage itself: ayat 27–28 describe people who *explicitly rejected the reckoning and utterly denied the Prophets* — which cannot describe people of Tawhid. A third group read ayat 24–25 as a circumstantial clause: for the countless aeons of the aḥqāb they will taste nothing but boiling water and pus, and when those ages are over the condition may change, and other kinds of punishment may be imposed. And whichever reading one takes, Maʿārif is emphatic that the notion of the disbelievers ever being released from Hell is contrary to the explicit texts and the common consent of the Ummah, and unworthy of consideration.

A report from Suddi, from Murrah ibn ʿAbdullah, captures the stakes with unforgettable force: if the inmates of Hell were told they would remain for the number of pebbles in the entire world, they would *rejoice* — because pebbles, though billions upon billions, are finite, so the torment would someday end. And if the people of Paradise were told they would remain for the count of those same pebbles, it would *sadden* them — because it would mean their bliss has an end (Mazhari). Eternity changes the meaning of every number.

## Nothing cool, nothing to drink (ayat 24–26)

Ayah 24 strips away the two things a burning person craves: **"There they will not taste any coolness or drink"** — no coolness for their hearts, Ibn Kathir says, and no wholesome drink to partake of. Then ayah 25 gives the bitter exception: **"except ḥamīm and ghassāq."** Abu Al-ʿAliyah noted the precision of the grammar: the ḥamīm is the exception to the *coolness*, and the ghassāq the exception to the *drink* — a reading Rabiʿ bin Anas shared. Each deprivation is answered by its own grotesque substitute.

*Ḥamīm* is water at its maximum heat and point of boiling — Maʿārif adds that brought near the face it would burn the flesh, and taken into the stomach it would cut the internal organs to pieces. *Ghassāq* is gathered from the pus, sweat, tears, and wound-washings of the people of Hellfire — and Ibn Kathir notes it is unbearably *cold*, with an intolerable stench, adding: "May Allah save us from that by His beneficence and grace."

Then comes the hinge of the whole passage, ayah 26: **jazāʼan wifāqā — "a fitting reward," an exact recompense.** Mujahid, Qatadah and others explained: what befalls them of this punishment corresponds precisely to the wicked deeds they were doing in this life. Maʿārif puts it plainly: the punishment is based on justice and equity — they will not be wronged in the least. This single phrase reframes everything before it. The horror of ayat 21–25 is not cruelty; it is correspondence.

## The crime beneath the punishment (ayat 27–29)

Why is it fitting? Ayat 27–28 name the two-part crime. First, **"they never expected any reckoning"** (ayah 27) — they did not believe there would be an abode in which they would be called to account. This was not a slip or a weakness; it was the operating assumption of their whole lives. A person who expects no audit lives accordingly. Second, **"they denied Our signs with utter denial"** (ayah 28) — they met Allah's evidences and proofs, revealed to His Messengers, "with rejection and obstinance" (Ibn Kathir). The word *kidhdhābā* is an emphatic verbal noun — total, wholesale rejection — and Ibn Kathir notes its unusual grammatical status as a verbal noun not derived from a verb, underscoring its intensity.

Against their denial of any accounting stands ayah 29: **"And We have everything recorded precisely."** Ibn Kathir paraphrases Allah's meaning: 'Surely We know the deeds of all creatures, and We have written these deeds for them, and We will reward them based upon this' — good for good, evil for evil. They refused to expect a reckoning; the reckoning, meanwhile, was being written down to the last detail. The Book they denied was already keeping their account.

## "So taste" (ayah 30)

The passage closes with a sentence addressed directly to the people of the Fire: **"So taste — for We will never increase you except in torment."** Ibn Kathir explains that it will be said to them: taste what you were in; you will never be increased in anything except torment matching its type of sin, and more of the same. Maʿārif adds the logic of the correspondence: in the world they went on adding disbelief upon disbelief — had death not overtaken them, they would have continued adding it forever — so today their punishment goes on being added. An unending sin of the heart meets an unending recompense.

Qatadah reported from Abu Ayyub Al-Azdi, from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr: "Allah did not reveal any Ayah against the people of the Hellfire worse than this Ayah" — *So taste; We shall not increase you except in torment* — "They will continue increasing in torment forever." For every other suffering, the sufferer's hope is that tomorrow may be lighter. Ayah 30 removes that hope: for the people of the Fire, tomorrow is only ever more.

## What the passage asks of us

The passage's own logic points to its lesson. The root of everything here is ayah 27 — *they never expected a reckoning*. The believer is the person who does expect it: who lives knowing that "all things We have recorded in a Book" (ayah 29) includes their own ledger, and that the recompense will be *wifāqā* — exactly fitting. And the sūrah does not leave the reader in the Fire: as Maʿārif notes, having depicted the punishment of the disbelievers, the verses that follow turn to depict the reward and blessings of the righteous. The ambush on the road is real — but so is the escort of the angels of reward, waiting on the same bridge for those who carry the permit of faith.

passages.title: The righteous rewarded with gardens and honor
passages.tafsir:
## The turn from terror to tenderness

After the sūrah's harrowing portrait of Hell and the rebellious who are told, "So now taste! We will never add to you anything except torment" (ayah 30), the scene changes completely. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the hinge exactly here: thus far the punishment of the disbelievers was depicted; as opposed to this, the reward and blessings of the righteous believers are now depicted. Ayat 31–36 are that counter-portrait — six short verses that move from the fact of the believers' triumph (ayah 31), through a sensory tour of what awaits them (ayat 32–34), to the atmosphere of the place (ayah 35), and finally to the source of it all: the Lord Himself (ayah 36). What holds the passage together is a single sentence in Arabic — everything from the gardens to the brimming cup is the unpacking of one word, *mafāz*.

## Ayah 31: What is a "mafāz"?

"Indeed, the righteous will have *mafāzan*" — rendered as "salvation" or "a success." The early authorities read the word in two complementary ways, both recorded by Ibn Kathir. Mujahid and Qatadah said it means "they are successful and thus, they are saved from the Hellfire" — escape itself is the triumph. Ibn ʿAbbās and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it names "a place of enjoyable recreation" — not merely getting out of danger, but arriving somewhere delightful. Ibn Kathir judges Ibn ʿAbbās's reading the more obvious one, and his reason is simply the flow of the passage: Allah immediately follows the word with gardens, vineyards, companions, and cups. The verses that follow are the contents of the *mafāz*.

The people who receive it are *al-muttaqīn* — those who have *taqwā*, the vigilant consciousness of Allah that guards a person against what displeases Him. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary by saying that Allah here "informs about the happy people and what He has prepared for them of esteem, and eternal pleasure." Note that word *esteem*: this passage is not only about pleasure but about honor — being received, hosted, and gifted by the Lord.

## Ayat 32–34: The contents of the triumph

**Gardens and vineyards (ayah 32).** The word *ḥadāʼiq*, Ibn Kathir explains, means gardens of palm trees and other things — and vineyards are named alongside them.

**Companions of equal age (ayah 33).** The phrase *kawāʿib atrāban* describes the maidens of Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid and others explained *kawāʿib* as describing their youthful, fully formed beauty — they will be virgins, equal in age. *Atrāb* means "of equal age": Ibn Kathir notes the early commentators' explanation that "they will only have one age" — a Paradise without decline, where nothing fades. He adds that fuller explanation of this was given under Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah.

**A brimming cup (ayah 34).** *Kaʼsan dihāqan* — "full cups of pure wine." The early authorities circle the word *dihāq* from slightly different angles, and Ibn Kathir records them all: Ibn ʿAbbās said "continuously filled" — it never runs low; ʿIkrimah said "pure"; Mujahid, Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd all said "completely filled." Put the readings together and you have a cup that is full, stays full, and holds nothing but what is clean. In this world a full cup is soon empty; the cup of Paradise is *dihāq* — filled without interruption.

## Ayah 35: What Paradise sounds like

Then a striking shift. After describing what Paradise contains, the Qurʼan describes it by what is *absent* from it: "never to hear any idle talk (*laghw*) or lying therein." Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's words about the cup of Paradise elsewhere: "Free from any laghw, and free from sin" (52:23). His comment: there will be no vain, worthless speech there, nor any sinful lying — "rather, it will be the abode of peace, and everything that is in it will be free of any shortcomings."

## Ayah 36: A reward that is a gift — the paradox at the heart of the passage

The passage closes by naming where all this comes from: *jazāʼan min rabbika ʿaṭāʼan ḥisābā* — "a fitting reward as a generous gift from your Lord."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something remarkable here. The verse uses two words that appear to pull against each other: *jazāʼ* (reward — something received in exchange for service) and *ʿaṭāʼ* (gift — something given gratis, unearned). Why both? Because, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the blessings of Paradise are a "reward" for its people only in appearance; in reality they are a Divine grant given freely — for no human's deeds could pay even for the blessings Allah already gave him in this world, let alone for the Hereafter, which depends entirely on Divine grace. It cites the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ that no one will enter Paradise merely by virtue of his deeds unless Allah shows His grace — and when the Companions asked, "What about you, Messenger of Allah?", he ﷺ replied that not even he would enter merely by virtue of his actions. Deeds are the condition; grace is the cause.

Then there is the closing word *ḥisābā*, and both commentaries open it up:

- **"Sufficient."** Ibn Kathir reads it through an Arab idiom: "He gave me and he sufficed me," meaning he provided for me until I needed nothing more — the same root that gives the believer's saying, *"Allah is sufficient for me."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the parallel idiom *aḥsabtu*: to give someone so much that he finally cries out, "Enough — this is too much for me!" The gift of ayah 36, then, is one that outruns its recipient's capacity to receive: in Ibn Kathir's words, "sufficient, suitable, comprehensive and abundant."
- **"Reckoned."** The second meaning Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records is "balancing of account," a measuring out. Mujahid held that the grant is given gratis, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it will nonetheless be proportioned — in keeping with each person's degree of sincerity, as reported in authentic Traditions. It illustrates this with the rank of the Companions: were a Companion to spend a single *mudd* (a small handful-measure, roughly 815 grams) in the way of Allah and a non-Companion to spend the equivalent of Mount Uḥud, the Companion's handful would weigh heavier.

So the one word carries both truths at once: the gift will be abundant beyond need, and it will be exquisitely fitted to who you were.

## Living it

The passage offers one door in: *taqwā*. Everything in ayat 32–36 is suspended from the single phrase "for the *muttaqīn*" in ayah 31. And ayah 36 quietly reorders the believer's inner life: work as if deeds matter — they are the stated grounds of the reward — while hoping in Allah's grace, not in the deeds themselves, since even the Prophet ﷺ pointed away from his own actions to Allah's grace. The mudd-versus-Uḥud comparison presses the point further: the grant is given in keeping with the degree of sincerity, so a small deed offered with a true heart may outweigh a mountain.

passages.title: The Lord's majesty and the final warning
passages.tafsir:
## The closing scene of Sūrat al-Nabaʼ

These four ayat are the final movement of Sūrat al-Nabaʼ. The sūrah has just finished describing the reward of the people of taqwā (ayat 31–36), ending with the words "a reward from your Lord, a sufficient gift." Now the camera pulls back, as it were, from the gift to the Giver: ayah 37 names Him — Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, al-Raḥmān — and the remaining ayat place us in His court on the Day of Judgement, where even the angels stand silent, and where the only wise response is stated plainly in ayah 39: take a path back to your Lord before the "near torment" of ayah 40 arrives. What holds the passage together is a single idea: the majesty of Allah on that Day, and the choice it forces on every listener now.

## Ayah 37: The Lord before whom none dares speak

Ibn Kathir explains that in this ayah "Allah informs of His magnificence and His majesty" — that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them and between them, and that He is *al-Raḥmān*, the Most Gracious, "Whose mercy covers all things." Notice the pairing: overwhelming lordship and overwhelming mercy in the same breath. The sūrah does not present a distant tyrant but the Merciful One — and yet precisely because of His majesty, "they cannot dare to speak" (*lā yamlikūna minhu khiṭāban* — literally, they possess no power of address before Him).

Ibn Kathir reads this to mean that no one is able to *begin* addressing Allah except by His permission, and he anchors it in two parallel ayat: "Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?" (2:255, Āyat al-Kursī) and "On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His leave" (11:105). Speech in that court — even intercession — is a granted privilege, never a right.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a subtle alternative reading. The sentence may be connected to the preceding ayah about reward ("a sufficing grant," 78:36): in that case it means that when Allah assigns each person a grade of reward, no one may question why one received more and another less. If the sentence is read on its own, it means that no one in the Plane of Gathering (the vast plain where creation is assembled for judgement) can speak to Him without His permission — and that permission, Maʿārif notes, will be granted in some stations of the Gathering and not in others. Both readings converge on the same reality: on that Day, all initiative belongs to Allah.

## Ayah 38: The Rūḥ and the angels in ranks — and who is the Rūḥ?

The scene sharpens: "the Day that al-Rūḥ and the angels will stand forth in rows, they will not speak except him whom al-Raḥmān allows, and he will speak what is right."

Who is *al-Rūḥ* ("the Spirit")? The scholars genuinely differed, and the sources present both views:

- **Jibrīl.** Ibn Kathir reports this from al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, supporting it with 26:193–194, where revelation is brought down by "the trustworthy Rūḥ… upon your heart." Muqātil bin Ḥayyān described him as "the noblest of the angels, the closest of them to the Lord, and the one who delivers the revelation." On this reading, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, Jibrīl is mentioned separately *before* the angels in general to signal the greatness of his rank.
- **A distinct creation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that according to certain Prophetic traditions the Rūḥ is not an angel at all but a huge army of Allah, beings with heads, hands and legs. On this interpretation there will be two rows on that Day: one row of the Rūḥ and one row of the angels.

Either way, the image is the point: the mightiest beings in creation — including the very angel who carried revelation to the prophets — stand in disciplined ranks, silent. If *they* do not speak without leave, what of us?

Ibn Kathir connects the exception clause ("except him whom al-Raḥmān allows") to the hadith confirmed in the Sahih, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "And none will speak on that Day except the Messengers." Even the prophets speak only within that granted permission.

And whoever is permitted "will speak what is right" (*ṣawāban*) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, the truth. Abu Salih and ʿIkrimah both noted that foremost among that truth is the declaration that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah. In a court where only truth may be uttered, the greatest truth of all is tawḥīd itself.

## Ayah 39: The True Day — and the open door

"That is the True Day" (*dhālika al-yawmu al-ḥaqq*). Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and absolute: it will come to pass and there is no avoiding it. The Day is not a matter of opinion or speculation. It is *ḥaqq* — real, certain, fixed.

Then, remarkably, the ayah turns from the courtroom to an invitation: "So whosoever wills, let him seek a place with His Lord" — a *maʼāb*. Ibn Kathir unpacks the word beautifully: a place of return, a path that leads to Him, a way one may travel to reach Him. The Day cannot be avoided, but the outcome can be chosen. The door back to the Lord stands open, and the ayah leaves the choice — "whosoever wills" — in the listener's hands.

## Ayah 40: The near torment, the deeds laid bare, and the cry "Would that I were dust!"

The sūrah ends with its final warning: "Verily, We have warned you of a near torment." Why "near," when centuries may pass? Ibn Kathir answers: it is called near to stress that its occurrence has drawn close, "because everything that is coming will certainly come to pass." Whatever is certain is, in the truest sense, already near.

**"The day when man will see that which his hands have sent forth."** Ibn Kathir explains that every deed will be presented to its doer — the good and the bad, the old and the new — and cites the parallels: "And they will find all that they did placed before them" (18:49) and "On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind" (75:13). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail on *how* one will "see" his deeds: either his ledger of deeds will be placed in his hands and he will read it, or — as certain narratives confirm — the deeds themselves will appear in the Plane of Gathering embodied in visible form. Maʿārif also records a third possibility, explained by Mazhari: "the day" may refer to the day of death, and the "seeing" takes place in the grave, in the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection). On any reading, the phrase "what his hands have sent forth" carries its own warning: what awaits each of us on that Day is nothing other than what we ourselves have dispatched ahead.

**"And the disbeliever will say: Would that I were dust!"** Ibn Kathir explains this cry: when the disbeliever sees the torment of Allah and looks at his wicked deeds recorded against him by the noble scribes among the angels, he will wish he had been mere dust — that he had never been created at all. The sources then relate the striking scene behind this wish. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Sayyidna ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿUmar that on the Day of Resurrection the earth will become one level plain on which human beings, jinn, domesticated animals and wild animals are all gathered. Animals that were wronged by other animals will be allowed their redress — if a horned goat wronged a hornless one, the wronged animal will take its due. Ibn Kathir puts it memorably: Allah will rectify matters between them "with His just wisdom that does not wrong anyone. Even the hornless sheep will be allowed to avenge itself against the sheep with horns." Then, when judgement between the animals is complete, Allah will say to them, "Be dust" — and they will become dust. Seeing this, the disbeliever will cry out, wishing he too had been an animal and could dissolve into dust, spared the reckoning and the punishment of Hell. Ibn Kathir notes that something of similar meaning is reported in the well-known hadith about the Ṣūr (the Trumpet), with narrations from Abu Hurayrah, ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, and others. Maʿārif closes the account with the plea every reader should echo: we seek refuge in Allah from it.

The scene teaches two things at once. First, the absolute justice of that Day — so thorough that even animals, who bear no religious responsibility, have their grievances settled. Second, the terrifying inversion it produces: existence itself, the very gift the disbeliever squandered, becomes the thing he longs to surrender.

## Living the passage

The sūrah does not leave its listener as a spectator. Ayah 39 has already told us what to do with all this: the Day is true, the torment is near in the only sense that matters, and the deeds now leaving our hands are exactly what we will meet again. "So whosoever wills, let him seek a place with His Lord" — a path of return taken now, while speech is still ours to offer freely, before the Day when none will speak except by the permission of al-Raḥmān.

With this ayah the commentary on Sūrat al-Nabaʼ ends — and, as Ibn Kathir concludes, all praise and thanks are due to Allah.
